scenes.tts: A virus waits on a light switch, then reaches a cell that makes new copies. Was the virus alive on the switch? Watch what each object can do, and who supplies the work.
scenes.visual: Hook first, no title. A blue schematic virus rests on a large switch at left. A fingertip carries it toward a pink host cell at right. Inside the cell, pale parts circulate continuously. On-screen question: Alive on the switch? COLOR MAP for both films: bacterium green, virus blue, host pink, genes purple, energy and carbon gold, neutral labels white.
scenes.narration: A virus waits on a light switch, then reaches a cell that makes new copies. Was the virus alive on the switch? Watch what each object can do, and who supplies the work.

scenes.visual: Brief title over the same moving world: Who Can Act Alone? The fingertip continues drifting toward the host cell; no frozen card.

scenes.tts: Biologists organize evidence with characteristics of life. Living things have cells, use energy, grow, respond, keep conditions steady, reproduce, and evolve. The list guides a decision. It is not a score where an individual tick wins.
scenes.visual: The switch slides aside. Seven white icons orbit the host cell: cell, energy arrow, growth arrow, response flash, steady gauge, copy, and generations. The icons keep circling. A single green check briefly enlarges, then shrinks under the label Not enough alone.
scenes.narration: Biologists organize evidence with characteristics of life. Living things have cells, use energy, grow, respond, keep conditions steady, reproduce, and evolve. The list guides a decision. It is not a score where an individual tick wins.

scenes.tts: Bring in a bacterium. It is a single cell with a membrane, cytoplasm, genes, and ribosomes. This prokaryote has no nucleus and, typically, no membrane-covered organelles. In suitable conditions, materials cross its membrane. Its ribosomes build proteins. It uses energy, grows, responds, and divides.
scenes.visual: A large green schematic bacterium fills the frame. Its membrane flexes, gold material blocks cross inward, and white ribosome workbenches move along purple gene instructions. The cell lengthens and divides into two. The orbiting life icons light green as each action occurs.
scenes.narration: Bring in a bacterium. It is a single cell with a membrane, cytoplasm, genes, and ribosomes. This prokaryote has no nucleus and, typically, no membrane-covered organelles. In suitable conditions, materials cross its membrane. Its ribosomes build proteins. It uses energy, grows, responds, and divides.

scenes.tts: Now bring back the virus. It carries genes inside a protein capsid, but it is not a cell. The capsid protects the genes. Some viruses add a fatty envelope outside the capsid. It has no cytoplasm or ribosomes. Outside a host, it does not take in food, use energy, or grow.
scenes.visual: The two bacteria slide left and become one. A blue schematic virus enlarges beside it. Its blue capsid opens like two labeled shells around one purple genes block. Empty spaces labeled no cytoplasm and no ribosomes remain visibly empty. Gold material flows past without entering.
scenes.narration: Now bring back the virus. It carries genes inside a protein capsid, but it is not a cell. The capsid protects the genes. Some viruses add a fatty envelope outside the capsid. It has no cytoplasm or ribosomes. Outside a host, it does not take in food, use energy, or grow.

scenes.tts: Predict what changes when the virus enters the host cell. Does the virus gain cell machinery, or does the host supply what it lacks? Keep your eye on the ribosomes.
scenes.visual: The blue virus approaches the pink host cell. Two possible paths appear: virus gains machinery, or host supplies what it lacks. The host's white ribosome workbenches continue moving. Large on-screen word: PREDICT.
scenes.narration: Predict what changes when the virus enters the host cell. Does the virus gain cell machinery, or does the host supply what it lacks? Keep your eye on the ribosomes.

scenes.visual: Hold the prediction question. The host membrane ripples and its ribosomes move slowly. A small thinking ring circles the two possible paths; reveal neither answer.

scenes.tts: The host supplies what the virus lacks. It provides ribosomes, energy, and building blocks. Viral genes use them to make virus parts. Host enzymes or viral enzymes copy the viral genes, depending on the virus. The parts assemble around the copies. The virus never gains its own metabolism.
scenes.visual: The host-supplies-what-it-lacks path glows. The virus enters the pink host and its blue capsid comes apart, releasing the purple genes block; no intact original virus remains inside the cell. The genes block moves beside the host's white ribosome workbenches. Gold energy arrows and pale building blocks feed the workbenches. A small white enzyme block, labeled host or viral enzyme, copies the purple block. New blue capsid pieces assemble around the copied purple blocks.
scenes.narration: The host supplies what the virus lacks. It provides ribosomes, energy, and building blocks. Viral genes use them to make virus parts. Host enzymes or viral enzymes copy the viral genes, depending on the virus. The parts assemble around the copies. The virus never gains its own metabolism.

scenes.tts: Edge cases show why a box cannot decide alone. A mature red blood cell cannot divide, yet it remains a cell. A crystal gets bigger, but it has no cells and no metabolism. Growth alone is not enough.
scenes.visual: The host world compresses upward. Below, a pink-red blood cell moves and bends through a narrow tube while its divide icon stays off. Beside it, a white schematic crystal gains repeating blocks. Labels appear: cell, no division; bigger, no cell.
scenes.narration: Edge cases show why a box cannot decide alone. A mature red blood cell cannot divide, yet it remains a cell. A crystal gets bigger, but it has no cells and no metabolism. Growth alone is not enough.

scenes.tts: Viruses carry genes and evolve, so scientists still discuss their place near life's edge. Virginia biology classes viruses as nonliving because they are not cells and have no metabolism of their own. They depend on a host cell to be copied.
scenes.visual: The red cell and crystal slide away. Generations of blue viruses drift along a branching purple path labeled evolves. A bracket labeled Virginia biology narrows attention to three carried icons: cell, metabolism, host dependence. Cell and metabolism stay empty for the virus; only host dependence lights.
scenes.narration: Viruses carry genes and evolve, so scientists still discuss their place near life's edge. Virginia biology classes viruses as nonliving because they are not cells and have no metabolism of their own. They depend on a host cell to be copied.

scenes.tts: Return to the switch. The virus can wait there and later be copied, but waiting is not living. The host cell supplies the ribosomes and energy. The bacterium carries its own cell machinery and can act when conditions suit it.
scenes.visual: Return to the original switch-host world. A blue virus rests on the switch. A green bacterium beside it takes in gold blocks and lengthens. A dotted arrow connects the virus to the pink host; a solid circular work arrow stays inside the bacterium.
scenes.narration: Return to the switch. The virus can wait there and later be copied, but waiting is not living. The host cell supplies the ribosomes and energy. The bacterium carries its own cell machinery and can act when conditions suit it.

scenes.tts: So ask these questions. Is it a cell, and does it have its own ribosomes and metabolism? That leads to the course rule. Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.
scenes.visual: The switch, host, bacterium, and virus settle into one comparison. Two question labels point to the green cell and blue virus. The bacterium's work arrow continues; the virus's arrow leads to the host.
scenes.narration: So ask these questions. Is it a cell, and does it have its own ribosomes and metabolism? That leads to the course rule. Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.

scenes.visual: End card shows one line only: 'Bacteria are living cells; viruses are not cells and are classed nonliving.' No subtitle, URL, title, or smaller line. Gentle green and blue ambient motion continues behind the text.
